title: The trust and safety tech stack: best tools for each layer in 2026
summary: The trust and safety tech stack, layer by layer: tools for verification, devices, fraud, moderation and cases. Sixtyfour researches who is behind accounts.
body_markdown:
It is the set of tools a platform uses to keep its accounts, content and transactions safe, usually built in layers that each answer one question. The common layers are identity verification at signup, device and network intelligence, fraud and risk decisioning, content moderation, case management and enforcement, threat intelligence, and account investigation into who is behind an account. Most teams add them one at a time, in the order their cases need them.


Two kinds of tool, working on different evidence. Device and fraud tools such as Fingerprint, Incognia, Sift, SEON, Sardine and Persona's Graph link accounts through signals your platform collects, such as the devices, sessions and transactions they share. Sixtyfour links them through what the operator reused outside your platform: it researches an account's email address, phone number, username or name across public sources and returns the other accounts and pages that share them, each with its source.


Yes. Sixtyfour is a research agent that takes the email address, phone number, username or name an account has used, researches public sources, and returns the person and the related accounts it finds, with a source for every finding and anything it could not establish reported as open. It does not see your platform's registration or log-in records, verify documents or fingerprint devices, so those stay with your own systems and the other layers, and a person on your team decides what happens to the account.


Device intelligence is usually the first line: Fingerprint recognises returning browsers and devices even after cookies are cleared, and Incognia lists account ban evasion among the problems it handles for delivery and ride-sharing apps. Fraud decisioning tools such as Sift and Sardine check new signups against fraud data drawn from across their customers. When an evader returns on a new device, Sixtyfour can link the new account to the removed one through a handle, email address or phone number reused on other sites, with the source for each link.


Start with the layer that matches the harm you see most: a moderation model if users post, fraud decisioning if money moves, and a place to record every decision, which can be the case features inside a tool you already use. Add device intelligence once banned users start coming back, identity verification where a fake identity is expensive, and account investigation once cases need to know who is behind an account.


Identity verification checks, at a moment such as signup, that a real person matches the identity document they present, using document checks, face matching and liveness detection. Account investigation usually starts after an account has been flagged, and asks who is behind it and what else they run, mostly from evidence outside your platform such as reused handles, email addresses and phone numbers. An account that passed verification can still be sold or taken over later, so most platforms that face repeat abuse use both.
